title: Independent ideas. Extraordinary finds.
intro: A daily selection of independent games and useful Android apps, with original F7 insights and links to their creators.

entries.name: ScreenPlink
entries.summary: ScreenPlink turns a matte monitor into a laser shooting range: a webcam watches the screen instead of you, finds the exact pixel your laser dot hits, draws the bullet hole and plays the shot. Targets fall, scores count and the magazine runs dry, entirely offline with no account and no ads. Full source ships with the build under Apache-2.0.
features: A webcam pointed at the monitor detects each laser hit at pixel level
Works with a laser training pistol or a laser bullet in a real firearm
Arcade loop with falling targets, scoring and a limited magazine
Runs fully offline with no account, no ads and no telemetry
Complete source code included with the build under Apache-2.0
entries.insight: Aiming a webcam at a screen instead of at a player is the whole trick, and it makes dry-fire practice measurable on hardware most people already own. An Apache-2.0 grant that explicitly allows commercial use is a generous touch for the gun shops and bars the README imagines as homes for it.

asset.attribution: ScreenPlink trailer still, from the vkorost/screenplink repository. Apache-2.0 license.
asset.alt: Two laser pistols firing at figures shown on a monitor in ScreenPlink

entries.name: Quorum
entries.summary: Quorum is an incremental systems-design game for software engineers. You start with one virtual machine in a garage, wire components onto a board, choose a language and runtime for each server, and fight one realistic bottleneck after another until the company serves billions and goes public. Every mechanic mirrors real system behavior, and the whole game runs in the browser with no account.
features: Mechanics model real behavior: PHP-FPM waits, Node event-loop stalls, JVM warm-up
Cache stampedes, hidden p99 latency and incident pressure arrive as you scale
Pick a language and runtime per server and wire components on a design board
A company lives in your browser and can be exported as text for backup
The companion wiki doubles as a free systems-design reference
entries.insight: Most idle games reward clicking; Quorum rewards capacity planning. The fiction never lies to you — queues fill, caches stampede and averages hide the p99 — so an evening of play quietly doubles as a refresher course in production engineering.

asset.attribution: Quorum hero image, from the elianiva/quorum repository. GPL-3.0 license.
asset.alt: Quorum hero art: grow a startup one bottleneck at a time

entries.name: Yarn Planet
entries.summary: Yarn Planet is a small-planet walking game that runs in the browser. You carry a spool bigger than your head across a pencil-sketch world, and every step lays down thread: connect the generator to the lighthouse, the spring to the waterwheel, a string of lights down the old street, and color floods back like watercolor as the town wakes up. No install; plays on desktop and phone.
features: Your walking path literally becomes the thread that powers the world
Reconnect power, water and street lights to bring color back to the planet
Color spreads like watercolor the moment a connection completes
Light multiplayer through preset greetings only, with no free-text chat
Plays in desktop and phone browsers with no installation
entries.insight: The map is the mechanic: you draw the circuit by walking it. That single idea carries the whole game, and the greeting-only multiplayer keeps the mood gentle without ever pretending to be a social network. The repository even documents how the planet was made, prompt by prompt.

asset.attribution: Yarn Planet trailer still, from the makerjackie/yarn-planet repository. MIT license.
asset.alt: A thread being carried across a pencil-sketch planet in Yarn Planet

entries.name: Snack Hole
entries.summary: Snack Hole drops a hungry hole into a bright low-poly city and asks it to eat its way up: cones, people, cars, houses, skyscrapers, cargo ships and jumbo jets all go down, feeding a deep incremental meta-game. Seven procedural maps ship with traffic, animals and events, 124 prop types, and dash, vortex and mega-mouth abilities. Play free in the browser on desktop, touch or gamepad.
features: Seven procedural maps with traffic, animals and city events
124 prop types scale from traffic cones to jumbo jets
Dash, vortex and mega-mouth abilities mapped to keyboard, touch and gamepad
A deep incremental meta-game feeds progression between runs
The repo includes unit tests and a balance simulator with pacing targets
entries.insight: The hole-that-eats-the-city formula is well worn, but this build is unusually serious about its engineering: type-checked builds, unit tests and a scripted balance harness sit behind the chaos, which is exactly what you want from a free, MIT-licensed arcade time-killer.

asset.attribution: Snack Hole screenshot, from the SamadiPour/snack-hole-game repository. MIT license.
asset.alt: A giant round hole swallowing a low-poly city in Snack Hole

entries.name: Deckdelve
entries.summary: Deckdelve is a free, open-source and fully offline Android version of Scoundrel, the solo card dungeon crawl by Zach Gage and Kurt Bieg. A 44-card deck deals four cards per room: resolve three and the fourth carries forward. The classic rules are kept faithful, every addition is opt-in, and a tutorial plus a rulebook walk you through a full run.
features: Faithful implementation of the classic Scoundrel solo rules
Each room deals four cards; you resolve three and the last carries over
All rule variants are opt-in toggles in Settings
Built-in tutorial and a rulebook with worked examples
Fully offline with F-Droid and GitHub release distribution
entries.insight: Adapting someone else's design this respectfully is rare: the credit is explicit, the classic rules stay intact, and new ideas arrive only as toggles. A perfect pocket dungeon crawl for commutes — no account, no network, no noise.

asset.attribution: Deckdelve app icon from the Fastlane metadata in the orumcan/Deckdelve repository. GPL-3.0 license.

entries.name: TA Reborn
entries.summary: TA Reborn is a clean-room reimplementation of the 1997 Total Annihilation engine, written from scratch in Rust. Point it at a copy of the original game you own and the same units, maps and campaigns fight again in a lit, living 3D world — with twenty thousand units in one battle and a cockpit view inside every one of them. Free for Windows, macOS and Linux.
features: Clean-room Rust engine that loads original Total Annihilation data you own
Twenty thousand units in a single battle, each with a cockpit view
Windows, macOS and Linux builds for x64 and ARM64
Community mods surface a click away in the integrated launcher
Free download from GitHub Releases and ta-reborn.com
entries.insight: Memory-safe Rust against a 1997 engine is a fun rematch, but the real achievement is scale: a cockpit inside every unit turns a classic RTS into a war movie you can step into. Clean-room method keeps it on the right side of the original's rights, in the best FOSS engine-remake tradition.

asset.attribution: TA Reborn social preview card, from the Jared-woodruff/TA-Reborn repository. GPL-3.0 license.
asset.alt: TA Reborn preview art of an armored assault at golden hour

entries.name: Restock
entries.summary: Restock is a free, open-source Android app that watches prices at the Australian supermarkets, bottle shops and chemists you choose, and tells you when a special is genuinely worth it, when to wait, and when to swap. No account, no ads and no tracking, on Android 8.0 or newer. A fresh release-candidate project from a single developer.
features: Tracks the supermarkets, bottle shops and chemists you actually use
Judges whether a special is real, worth waiting for, or swappable
No account, no ads, no tracking — data stays local
Runs on Android 8.0 and newer
GPL-3.0 with releases published on GitHub
entries.insight: Half-price claims deserve auditing, and this app does the audit for one country's grocery market with unusual focus. It is brand new and tiny, which is precisely the kind of early, useful work a daily discovery column exists to surface.

asset.attribution: Restock app icon from the d-plenty/Restock repository. GPL-3.0 license.

entries.name: PhoneBox
entries.summary: PhoneBox turns an old Android phone into a live desk panel for a Windows, Linux or macOS computer: widgets for PC performance, AI coding sessions, music, weather and anything you push to it yourself. The phone pairs over USB or Wi-Fi with no cloud in between, and a browser demo lets you try the panel before installing anything.
features: Widgets show PC stats, AI coding sessions, music and weather
Custom HTML widgets run sandboxed; Home Assistant entities can be switched
Pairs over USB or Wi-Fi with no cloud service
Android 9+ companion app with a .NET 10 desktop agent
A live browser demo previews the panel before setup
entries.insight: Every household has a retired phone in a drawer; this project gives it a job a smart display would charge for. Sandboxed custom widgets keep the DIY surface safe, which is the hard part of making second-screen gadgets approachable.

asset.attribution: PhoneBox hero image from the ersinkoc/phonebox repository. MIT license.
asset.alt: PhoneBox desk panel widgets shown on a phone next to a computer

entries.name: Tellyscope
entries.summary: Tellyscope manages an Android TV from your phone: debloat the launcher's clutter, install apps, and browse or transfer files on the TV, all without root and without a PC. The app is about 3 MB, ships in six languages, and an advanced monitor reports free space, CPU, RAM and network speed for the TV.
features: Debloat and manage an Android TV with no root access needed
Install apps and browse or transfer files from the phone
Advanced monitor shows free space, CPU, RAM and network speed
Small 3 MB app translated into six languages
Google Play, Obtainium and signed GitHub APK releases
entries.insight: Android TV boxes collect bloat the way boats collect barnacles, and nobody wants a keyboard on the couch. A phone-side control panel with no root requirement is the practical fix, and the signed-APK release channel keeps it installable on any box.

asset.attribution: Tellyscope app icon from the man15h/tellyscope repository. GPL-3.0 license.

entries.name: Cicada
entries.summary: Cicada brings live subtitles, two-way interpreting and AI meeting notes to Mac, Windows, Linux and Android. Every call and stream gets bilingual transcripts; you can speak back and be heard in another language, and all four apps share one meeting record format. The download page states it plainly: free and open source, with a SHA-256 checksum for every file.
features: Real-time subtitles and bilingual transcripts for meetings and streams
Two-way interpreting so you can answer in your own language
AI meeting notes with one shared record format across four apps
On Apple silicon, recording and recognition run fully on the machine
Free and open source downloads with per-file SHA-256 checksums
entries.insight: Cross-platform live interpretation is usually a subscription product; Cicada ships it as an open-source suite and publishes checksums, which is exactly the kind of operational care that builds trust in a tool that hears everything you say.

asset.attribution: Cicada app icon from the wquguru/cicada repository. Apache-2.0 license.

entries.name: Seca
entries.summary: Seca is three Android apps — Contacts, Phone and Messages — that share one Material 3 Expressive design and one philosophy: no account, no server, no Google. Seca Contacts has no Internet permission at all, so your address book physically cannot leave the phone, while DAVx5 or another sync of your choice can still reach it. Requires Android 12 or newer.
features: Seca Contacts runs with zero Internet permission by design
Phone and Messages share the same Material 3 Expressive design
No account, no server and no Google dependency anywhere
The address book stays reachable for DAVx5 or your chosen sync
All three apps are published on F-Droid and GitHub
entries.insight: Privacy claims usually end in a privacy policy; Seca makes its claim an operating-system fact by simply never asking for the permission. Enforcing privacy architecturally is the strongest form of the argument, and a unified Material 3 design keeps it pleasant to actually use.

asset.attribution: Seca Contacts app icon from the arditore/Seca repository. GPL-3.0-or-later; Seca Messages is AGPL-3.0-or-later.

entries.name: Tapbar
entries.summary: Tapbar creates tappable screen zones that open apps, trigger more than a hundred quick actions, and hand tasks to your favorite automation app. It runs completely offline, stays battery-efficient, and carries no ads or trackers. Distribution runs through F-Droid and GitHub releases under an MIT license.
features: Draw tappable zones anywhere on the screen to launch apps
More than 100 built-in quick actions
Bridges into third-party automation apps for custom routines
Fully offline and battery-efficient operation
No ads and no trackers, MIT-licensed on F-Droid
entries.insight: Gesture navigation traded reachability for screen space; Tapbar quietly gives you both by making empty screen corners tappable. It is a small idea executed precisely, and it changes how a phone feels in one hand.

asset.attribution: Tapbar store icon from the Earendel-lab/Tapbar repository. MIT license.

entries.name: Streak
entries.summary: Streak is a minimal, private habit tracker that gets out of the way: log a habit in a single tap, watch the streak grow, and open statistics only when you want them. Everything stays on the device — no account, no ads, no analytics and no servers. The README states the promise outright: free, open source and free of ads, and it stays that way.
features: One-tap habit logging with a growing streak view
Statistics and insights appear only when you ask for them
Optional habit timers for routines that need one
All data stays on the device with no account or servers
Flutter app translated into five languages on F-Droid
entries.insight: Habit trackers are a saturated genre, and Streak competes by subtraction: one tap, one flame, everything else optional. The README's promise that it stays free is exactly the kind of manifesto a small tool can actually keep.

asset.attribution: Streak launcher icon from the InlitX/streak repository. GPL-3.0 license.
